prompt: Scientist 1 would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

choices.text: The iridium in the boundary clay layer came from material outside the Earth.
choices.rationale: Correct. Scientist 1 says iridium is rare in the crust but common in asteroids, pointing to an extraterrestrial source.

choices.text: Dinosaur populations declined gradually over hundreds of thousands of years.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 describes a sudden event; gradual decline is Scientist 2's claim.

choices.text: The iridium in the boundary clay layer was carried up from deep inside the Earth.
choices.rationale: This is Scientist 2's explanation for the iridium, not Scientist 1's.

choices.text: The crater beneath the coast of Mexico formed long after the extinction.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 stresses that the crater and the layer are the same age.

explanation: Scientist 1 uses the iridium layer as evidence of an asteroid, so the iridium must come from outside the Earth.

stimulus.title: The End of the Dinosaurs
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
An asteroid about 10 km wide struck the Earth 66 million years ago. The impact threw enormous amounts of dust and sulfur into the air, which blocked sunlight for months. Plants died, and the animals that depended on them starved. The clearest evidence is a thin layer of clay found at sites around the world that is rich in iridium, an element rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids. The layer sits exactly at the boundary where dinosaur fossils stop appearing. A crater of the right age and size has also been identified beneath the coast of Mexico. Because the layer and the crater are the same age, the impact must have been the main cause of the extinction.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Massive volcanic eruptions in what is now India were the main cause. These eruptions released lava over an area larger than many countries and continued for hundreds of thousands of years. They poured carbon dioxide and sulfur gases into the atmosphere, causing rapid swings in climate and acid rain. Fossil records show that some groups of animals were already declining before the boundary layer formed, which an instant impact cannot explain. Iridium can also be carried up from deep within the Earth by such eruptions. An asteroid may have struck near the end, but it hit a world whose ecosystems were already collapsing from volcanic activity.

prompt: Scientist 1 and Scientist 2 would both most likely agree that:

choices.text: the Moon has an iron core as large, relative to its size, as Earth's.
choices.rationale: Both describe the Moon's core as small.

choices.text: the Moon formed from debris produced by a collision.
choices.rationale: Only Scientist 1 proposes a collision.

choices.text: the Moon's orbit is not tilted relative to Earth's equator.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 states the orbit is tilted; Scientist 1 does not dispute this.

choices.text: the Moon's rocks have oxygen isotope ratios similar to Earth's.
choices.rationale: Correct. Both accept the isotope match and offer different explanations for it.

explanation: The isotope similarity is a shared fact; each scientist explains it differently.

stimulus.title: The Origin of the Moon
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The Moon formed when a body about the size of Mars collided with the young Earth. The collision blasted molten rock from Earth's outer layers into orbit, where it quickly gathered into the Moon. This explains why the Moon's rocks match Earth's in the ratios of oxygen isotopes, which differ from one body to another in the solar system. It also explains why the Moon has a very small iron core: the impact stripped mostly rocky material from the outside of the Earth, leaving Earth's iron core behind. The Moon's rocks are also unusually dry, as expected if they were once heated enough to drive off their water.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The Moon formed elsewhere in the solar system and was captured by Earth's gravity as it passed nearby. Capture explains why the Moon is so large compared with Earth; the impact scenario should have left a much smaller moon or none at all, as computer models of similar collisions often show. The matching oxygen isotopes could result from the Moon forming in the same region of the solar system as Earth, from the same raw material. A capture would have left the Moon in a tilted orbit, and the Moon's orbit is indeed tilted relative to Earth's equator. The small core could simply reflect the Moon's original composition.

prompt: Suppose each of the following were discovered. Which one would most strengthen Scientist 1's position?

choices.text: Ice-core records show carbon dioxide levels beginning to fall well before global temperatures start to fall.
choices.rationale: Carbon dioxide falling first supports Scientist 2's view that it drives the cooling.

choices.text: Climate models show that small changes in sunlight cannot, by themselves, grow large ice sheets.
choices.rationale: This is Scientist 2's objection to the orbital explanation.

choices.text: Ocean circulation is found to change sharply just before each ice age.
choices.rationale: Circulation changes releasing or absorbing carbon dioxide fit Scientist 2's account.

choices.text: Ice ages are found to begin only at minima of northern summer sunlight, whatever the carbon dioxide level.
choices.rationale: Correct. Ice ages tied to sunlight minima independent of carbon dioxide make the orbital cycles the controlling factor.

explanation: Scientist 1 claims sunlight changes control ice ages; a finding that ice ages track sunlight minima regardless of carbon dioxide supports that.

stimulus.title: What Drives the Ice Ages
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Ice ages are driven by slow, regular changes in Earth's orbit and tilt. Over tens of thousands of years, the shape of Earth's orbit, the tilt of its axis, and the direction the axis points all shift in predictable cycles. These cycles change how much summer sunlight reaches the far northern lands. When northern summers are cool, winter snow does not fully melt, ice sheets grow, and their bright surfaces reflect still more sunlight. Records from deep-sea sediments show that the timing of past ice ages matches the periods of the orbital cycles. The cycles are the pacemaker; everything else follows.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Orbital cycles are too weak to produce ice ages on their own. The change in sunlight they cause is small, and it is spread across the year. The real driver is carbon dioxide. Air bubbles trapped in ancient ice show that carbon dioxide levels fell during every ice age and rose during every warm period, and carbon dioxide is far better than orbital changes at shifting the whole planet's temperature. The gas moves between the oceans and the atmosphere as ocean circulation changes, which can be triggered by many things. Orbital cycles may set the timing, but carbon dioxide does the work of cooling the globe.

prompt: Suppose careful dating showed that the great majority of the lava in India erupted after the iridium layer formed. This finding would most likely:

choices.text: support Scientist 2's claim that animals were declining before the boundary formed.
choices.rationale: Eruptions that came later cannot explain declines that came earlier.

choices.text: show that the crater beneath Mexico is older than the iridium layer.
choices.rationale: The finding concerns the lava, not the crater's age.

choices.text: weaken Scientist 1's view that the impact was the main cause of the extinction.
choices.rationale: The timing of the lava says nothing against the impact; if anything it removes a rival explanation.

choices.text: weaken Scientist 2's view that volcanic eruptions caused the extinction.
choices.rationale: Correct. If most eruptions came after the extinction, they could not have been its main cause.

explanation: Scientist 2 needs the eruptions to precede and overlap the extinction; eruptions mostly afterward undercut that.

prompt: Scientist 1's viewpoint would be most weakened by which of the following findings?

choices.text: Warm winters have become more frequent on the ridge.
choices.rationale: Warm winters are part of Scientist 1's account.

choices.text: Trees attacked by very large numbers of beetles die even when they are otherwise healthy and vigorous.
choices.rationale: Mass attacks overwhelming healthy trees is Scientist 1's claim.

choices.text: Beetle galleries are found beneath the bark of every dead pine.
choices.rationale: Galleries are Scientist 1's own evidence.

choices.text: Ridge pines removed before beetles emerged were replaced by new deaths at the same rate the next year.
choices.rationale: Correct. If removing infested trees does not slow the deaths, the beetles are not controlling the outcome, contrary to Scientist 1's view and remedy.

explanation: Scientist 1's remedy follows from beetles being the cause; its failure undercuts that view.

stimulus.title: The Dying Pines
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The pines on the ridge are dying because of bark beetles. The beetles bore through the bark and lay eggs, and their larvae eat the living layer beneath, cutting off the flow of water and sugar. Every dead tree examined shows the winding galleries the larvae leave, and traps caught ten times more beetles this year than five years ago. Warm winters now let the beetles survive and produce two generations in a summer instead of one. Healthy trees can drown attacking beetles in resin, but a mass attack overwhelms even vigorous trees. Removing infested trees before the beetles emerge is the way to protect the rest of the stand.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The underlying cause is drought. Rainfall on the ridge has been below average for six of the past eight years, and the soil there is thin and holds little water. A tree short of water cannot make enough resin to repel beetles, so the insects succeed on trees that would normally resist them. Trees on the well-watered lower slopes carry the same beetles yet remain mostly alive, and tree rings from the dead pines show narrow growth for several years before the beetles arrived. Beetles are the final blow, not the cause. Unless the drought ends or the stand is thinned so that fewer trees compete for water, removing infested trees will not save the others.

prompt: Scientist 1 would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

choices.text: The temperature difference is greater on holidays than it is on busy weekdays.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 says the difference shrinks on holidays; Scientist 1 does not discuss it.

choices.text: The temperature difference is largest in winter, when heating systems run.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 says the difference is smallest in winter.

choices.text: Replacing pavement with vegetation would lower nighttime temperatures in the city.
choices.rationale: Correct. Scientist 1 says vegetation cools the air and recommends planting trees.

choices.text: Waste heat from vehicles and buildings is the main reason the city is warm at night.
choices.rationale: This is Scientist 2's explanation.

explanation: Scientist 1 attributes the warmth to materials and the loss of vegetation, so adding vegetation should help.

stimulus.title: The Warm City
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The city center is about 4°C warmer at night than the surrounding farmland because of what the city is made of. Asphalt, brick, and concrete absorb sunlight during the day and store the heat, releasing it slowly after sunset. These surfaces are also dark, so they reflect less sunlight than fields and forests do. Vegetation cools the air as water evaporates from leaves, but the city has replaced most plants with pavement. The temperature difference is largest on clear, calm summer nights, when stored heat is released most effectively, and smallest in winter, when the sun is weak. Painting roofs white and planting trees would reduce the difference.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The warmth comes mainly from the energy people use. Every engine, air conditioner, furnace, and light releases heat into the city's air. In the dense center, this waste heat per square kilometer can rival the energy delivered by sunlight. The nighttime difference is large because the city keeps releasing heat after the sun sets, while the countryside does not. The difference also grows on weekdays, when traffic and business activity are heaviest, and shrinks on holidays, something that building materials alone cannot explain. Reducing energy use and improving the efficiency of vehicles and buildings would do more than changing roof colors.

choices.text: weekday traffic is what drives the temperature difference.
choices.rationale: Only Scientist 2 cites weekday traffic.

explanation: The observation being explained, a warmer city at night, is shared; the cause is disputed.

prompt: Which of the following best describes the main point on which the scientists disagree? They disagree about:

choices.text: whether a hole actually opened beneath the surface of Carver Road.
choices.rationale: Both accept that the collapse occurred.

choices.text: whether the void beneath the road formed slowly in rock or quickly in soil.
choices.rationale: Correct. Slow dissolving of limestone versus rapid washing of soil is the central dispute.

choices.text: whether a water main runs beneath the road at the site of the collapse.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 does not deny the main exists; the dispute is about its role.

choices.text: whether limestone can be dissolved by slightly acidic water over long periods.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 does not dispute the chemistry, only its relevance here.

explanation: The disagreement concerns the process and timescale that created the void.

stimulus.title: The Collapse at Carver Road
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The sudden hole that opened beneath Carver Road formed because rainwater slowly dissolved the limestone beneath the surface. Limestone is made of a mineral that dissolves in slightly acidic water, and rain becomes acidic as it absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and soil. Over thousands of years, water seeping down through cracks widened them into a cavern. The roof of the cavern thinned until it could no longer hold up the road. Caves and springs are common in the surrounding countryside, and the hole has sheer walls of solid limestone, exactly as expected when a cavern roof gives way.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The hole formed because a leaking water main washed away the soil beneath the road. The main, installed sixty years ago, runs directly under the collapse and was found to be cracked. Escaping water carried fine soil particles into a nearby storm drain, leaving a growing void just below the pavement. Limestone caverns take thousands of years to form, but the road showed no sign of sinking until two months before the collapse, soon after water pressure in the main was raised. The hole's walls are mostly loose soil, and the solid rock lies several meters deeper. Repairing the main is the key to preventing another collapse.

prompt: Which of the following is an assumption made by both scientists? Both assume that:

choices.text: the bleaching was caused by the reef's environment rather than by a disease of the corals.
choices.rationale: Correct. Each explanation names an environmental change; neither considers an internal disease of the coral.

choices.text: the water over the reef was warmer during the bleaching year than in any previous summer on record.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 says the corals had survived warmer summers.

choices.text: the corals will not recover once they have bleached.
choices.rationale: Neither scientist discusses recovery.

choices.text: sediment from the river reached every part of the reef.
choices.rationale: Only Scientist 2 discusses sediment, and only near the river.

explanation: Both explanations look outside the coral for the cause, taking for granted that an environmental change is responsible.

stimulus.title: The Bleaching Reef
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The reef bleached because the water became too warm. Corals live with tiny algae inside their tissues that supply most of their food and give them their color. When water temperature stays more than about one degree above the summer maximum for several weeks, the partnership breaks down: the coral expels the algae and turns white. Satellite records show that the sea surface over the reef was unusually warm for six weeks before the bleaching, and the most heavily bleached patches were in shallow water, where the water warmed most. Reefs far from any town or farm bleached in the same weeks, which only a regional cause such as temperature can explain.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The main cause was runoff from the land. Heavy rains in the months before the bleaching carried soil, fertilizer, and sewage from the coast onto the reef. Sediment clouds the water and settles on the corals, smothering them, while nutrients feed seaweeds that overgrow the coral and bacteria that attack its tissue. Water samples near the river mouth showed nutrient levels several times higher than normal, and bleaching was most severe on the parts of the reef closest to the river. Warm water can stress corals, but these corals had survived warmer summers before. The difference this year was the condition of the water, not its temperature alone.

prompt: Scientist 1's viewpoint would be most weakened by which of the following findings?

choices.text: Sensors show the sway reached full strength before any pedestrian had stepped onto the deck.
choices.rationale: Correct. Motion that begins before anyone is on the bridge cannot be caused by walkers.

choices.text: Video shows the walkers widening their stance and stepping in time with the motion of the deck.
choices.rationale: Synchronized stepping is consistent with Scientist 1.

choices.text: The sway was never observed on days when fewer than fifty people were on the bridge at one time.
choices.rationale: Dependence on crowd size supports Scientist 1.

choices.text: The sway stopped shortly after the bridge was closed to pedestrians.
choices.rationale: Stopping when cleared supports Scientist 1.

explanation: Scientist 1's cause is the crowd; sway before the crowd arrived contradicts it.

stimulus.title: The Swaying Footbridge
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The bridge swayed from side to side on its opening day because of the people walking on it. When a crowd walks across a flexible bridge, small sideways movements make people adjust their steps to keep their balance. Many walkers end up stepping in time with the sway, and their combined footsteps push the bridge at exactly the frequency at which it naturally rocks. The more the bridge moves, the more people fall into step, so the motion grows. The sway appeared only when the crowd was large and stopped within minutes when the crowd was cleared, and no sway has been measured on windy days when the bridge was empty.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The sway was caused by wind. As wind flows past the bridge deck and cables, it sheds swirling eddies alternately from each side, producing a push that switches direction at a regular rate. If that rate matches a natural frequency of the bridge, the structure rocks in resonance. The opening day was breezy, and the deck's flat shape is well suited to shedding eddies. Pedestrians certainly felt the motion and reacted to it, but their steps were a response to the sway, not its cause. Adding fins to the deck to break up the eddies, rather than limiting the crowd, is the correct fix.
